content:
How I Tried to Make Real Money with OpenAI’s Codex Agent on GitHub Bounties

On May 10, 2026, I saw a post from @chatgpt21 claiming that OpenAI’s new autonomous coding agent, Codex, had solved a GitHub bounty completely by itself and earned real money.

The post went viral.

So I decided to test it immediately.

What followed was a two-hour live experiment that showed me both the massive potential and the current limitations of using AI agents to hunt, solve, and submit paid open-source bounties.

This was not theory.

This was Codex searching for bounties, analyzing repositories, writing code, running tests, and preparing a pull request while I watched.

Setting Up Codex: The Practical Way

Getting started was surprisingly simple:

Go to chatgpt . com/codex, or select Codex inside ChatGPT.

Connect your GitHub account through OAuth.
Decide which repositories Codex can access.
Give it a clear autonomous objective.

My first prompt was simple.

¬ The Basic Autonomous Prompt:

_

Activate Goal / Autonomous mode.

Connect to my GitHub repositories.

Search for open issues that have bounties or monetary rewards using keywords like $100, $200, bounty, reward, paid, or sponsored.

Prioritize the easiest ones under $500.

Solve them completely on your own: write the code, pass all tests, open a clean Pull Request, and notify me when it is merged and the payment arrives.

_

Codex immediately switched into developer mode and started working.

But after a while, I realized that the prompt needed much more structure.

¬ The Optimized “Bounty Hunter” Prompt

Later in the session, Codex helped refine the instructions into a much stronger version.

This is the prompt that actually worked better:

_

Act as an open-source bounty development agent.

Objective: Find issues with real monetary rewards on GitHub, Algora, Polar, or Gitcoin that match my skill profile and solve one of them completely and professionally.

Criteria:

Prioritize bounties up to $500.
Prioritize repositories with good documentation, clear tests, and recent activity.
Avoid security issues, payments, cryptography, critical infrastructure, or overly large changes.
Before writing any code, first summarize:
Reward amount
Estimated difficulty
Tech stack
Risk level
Exact steps to solve it

Then clone the repository, create a new branch, implement a high-quality fix, run all tests, and prepare a clean Pull Request.

Never spam or submit low-effort PRs.

Only submit professional, high-quality solutions.

_

This changed everything.

The agent became much more disciplined.

Instead of rushing into code, it started evaluating opportunities, filtering risky tasks, checking repository quality, and thinking like a serious contributor.

¬ What Codex Actually Achieved

In a single session, Codex managed to:

Scan multiple bounty platforms in real time.

Search across Algora, GitHub, Polar, and Gitcoin.

Filter out saturated, risky, or low-quality bounties.

Identify a clean $100 bounty involving TypeScript, Cloudflare Workers, and integration testing.

Clone the repository.

Analyze the project structure, existing tests, and configuration.

Create a local branch.

Implement solid test coverage for successful flows, edge cases, and invalid payloads.

Run the complete test suite locally.

Confirm that all tests passed.

Prepare a professional Pull Request draft with a clear title, description, and reference to the original issue.

¬ The most impressive part?

It did most of this autonomously while I simply observed.

This felt very different from using a chatbot.

It felt closer to supervising a junior developer who can read documentation, inspect a codebase, run commands, make decisions, and explain what it is doing.

¬ The Reality Check: The Roadblocks

However, the experiment also exposed some serious limitations.

:: Safety Filters

The first major issue appeared when Codex started working with Cloudflare Workers and AI vector bindings.

Even though the task was only related to writing tests, the system triggered an internal warning:

“This content was flagged for possible cybersecurity risk.”

At that point, the agent was forced to stop.

This is one of the biggest limitations of cloud-based coding agents today.

They are powerful, but they operate inside strict safety boundaries. Sometimes those boundaries make sense. Other times, they interrupt harmless development work.

¬ Usage Limits and Credits

After roughly 90 minutes of heavy autonomous work, Codex hit the plan limit (20$ / month).

During that time, it had been cloning repositories, reading files, running commands, searching the web, analyzing issues, and preparing code.

Eventually, the session stopped because the quota had been reached.

This is another important reality: autonomous agents consume resources quickly.

If you use them seriously, limits and credits become part of the workflow.

¬ Bounty Saturation

The third problem was more human than technical.

After Codex had already done the work, it discovered that the chosen bounty had several open Pull Requests from other contributors.

Submitting another PR would probably have created unnecessary noise.

And that is exactly what serious contributors should avoid.

The goal is not to flood maintainers with AI-generated pull requests.

The goal is to submit high-quality, useful, professional contributions.

¬ Key Lessons from the Experiment

This short test taught me several important things.

First, Codex can already perform a large part of the work that a mid-level developer would do on small and medium-sized bounties.

It can search, read, clone, analyze, code, test, and prepare a PR.

Second, prompt engineering matters a lot.

The “summarize first, then act” structure dramatically improved the quality of the agent’s decisions.

Instead of blindly coding, Codex started acting like a disciplined technical contributor.

Third, cloud-based agents still have hard constraints.

They are limited by:

Safety filters

Usage quotas

Cost

Platform restrictions

Competition from other users

The quality of the repositories they work on

¬ The Future: Local AI Agents That Actually Pay You

Today, Codex is one of the most capable cloud coding agents available.

But it is still a paid cloud service with guardrails, quotas, and limits.

The real breakthrough may come from local open-source coding models.

With enough RAM and the right setup, developers can already run powerful coding models locally in efficient quantized formats.

Models such as Qwen Coder, DeepSeek Coder, MiniMax, and other Mixture-of-Experts systems are moving extremely fast.

:: The direction is clear:

Local agents will become cheaper, faster, more private, and less limited.

Soon, developers will run multiple local agents in parallel.

One agent could search GitHub issues.

Another could monitor Algora.

Another could inspect Polar bounties.

Another could evaluate difficulty and risk.

Another could open a branch, implement the solution, run tests, and prepare a professional PR.

This will not be fully passive income.

You will still need judgment, technical review, and ethical standards.

But it could become semi-autonomous income for developers who know how to combine:

Strong coding models

Good prompts

Local inference

Agent frameworks

Testing discipline

Responsible open-source contribution

¬ My Honest Take

The experiment did not make me money immediately.

But it showed me something more important:

The workflow is real.
The tools are close.
The opportunity is early.

Codex already feels like a serious software development assistant. 

But the next step is even more interesting: local AI agents that can work continuously without monthly limits, safety interruptions, or cloud dependency.

The future of AI-assisted earning will not belong to people who simply ask chatbots for code.

It will belong to people who know how to design autonomous workflows.

Not spam.

Not low-effort PRs.

Not fake automation.

Real agents.

Real repositories.

Real tests.

Real pull requests.

Real value.

The era of “AI employees that pay their own salary” is no longer science fiction.

It is starting now.

And the developers who learn how to control these agents early will have a serious advantage.

The tools are already here.

Now it is time to make them work.

content:
AI advertising is fundamentally changing.

Before, the logic was simple:

👉 you search something, platforms show you something.

Now AI systems are increasingly deciding distribution based on:

full context
user intent
conversation history
workflow stage

Which means:

AI is no longer just a traffic layer —
it’s becoming a revenue distribution system.

Whoever owns user context
will likely control future AI-native value distribution.

And that revenue won’t stop at advertising.

It expands into:

AI workflows, agent execution, payments, recommendations, automation services…

In other words,
AI is forming an entirely new income system.

But today, most people can only participate through company valuations and price appreciation —
not the underlying AI-native income itself.

That’s part of what Kvoucher is exploring:

If AI will generate massive onchain and offchain revenue in the future,
can those future cash flows be structured early and opened to broader participation?
